reviews.review: Since 2013, I have fallen in love with this game and have spent hundreds of hours just playing/grinding. The developers are constantly updating the game and have a great community team willing to listen to players of the game. With the recent release of the Fortuna update, it really shows how the developers take the issues of the game/last update and fix it with the next. These large updates don't come out very often, but it's worth the wait when they do come out, as they have exceeded our expectations. There are so many systems and different weapon varieties that even some veteran members still have more to explore. Sadly, since there are so many, it makes new players seem like they have to grind hours into the game just to earn these rewards. Now onto this topic, all rewards in the game can either be bought with platinum, or can crafted just by simply playing the game. It seems now that there are very few games and Triple A titles that release a product without microtransactions, but Warframe manages to shine out of the rest of the games and sets itself as an example for new developers and games to release in the future. I personally recommend that everybody should give the game a little try, just to see if it fits their tastes or not.

Ever wonder what happened to Digital Extremes, the other half that worked with Epic Games on the Unreal franchise? They’ve been having a rough time of it, it seems. Their third person shooter Dark Sector was met with mixed reviews and quickly forgotten. They helped 2K with the PS3 version of BioShock, and were then tasked with creating the tacked-on multiplayer portion of BioShock 2. From there, they developed the ill-fated Homefront, the underappreciated The Darkness II, and then the rushed and buggy movie tie-in game Star Trek: Into Darkness. After such a long and rocky road, it’s no surprise to see them seek refuge in the untapped frontier that is the Free To Play market. 

Warframe is a kind of spiritual success to Dark Sector. You play as a Tenno, an ancient warrior awoken from a very long cryosleep into a universe at war. The Grineer - humanoid clones with degenerate genes - want to rule it all. The Corpus, being a mega corporation with robots, wants to own it all. The Infested, infected with the “Tenocyte” virus that turns them into biological weapons, want to be everything. So the Tenno are tasked with saving the universe from this crapstorm.

The game has been in open beta since early 2013, but Update 14 has finally brought it into what I consider a “reviewable” state. Keep in mind free to play games update frequently, and so change dramatically often. Update 14 brought a much-needed tutorial prologue chapter and the entire user interface has been overhauled. The core game is mostly unchanged, but there was very little wrong with it to begin with. After selecting a mission, you (and friends or strangers) are dropped into a procedurally generated map. There, it’s all third-person action combat with wall-running, sliding, shooting while sliding, leaps, backflips and sweet melee combat. As you earn experience, your “frame”, weapons and companions (like a combat-capable space-dog pet you earn via a quest) level up, gaining more slots for Mods. Mods add various effects to your attacks, like fire damage, more ammo, or give you special moves.

There are many mission types, and missions may have random effects added to them like fire damage across the map, or a sudden Infested outbreak so you’re fighting them along with whoever is supposed to be there. Special effects randomly trigger around the solar system, which give you an opportunity for bigger rewards at higher risk. Warframe follows the Monster Hunter formula of farming specific bosses for the plans to craft certain weapons or frames. You can buy frames or weapons with real money, but everything can be earned in-game if you’re patient, except for fancy cosmetic items like space-scarves.
Get's repetitive and boring from time to time but okay in general i guess...
